original:
Scenario: A CMS sends live updates via a webhook/event pipeline.
Events include, but are not limited to:
- Add → new entities are being created.
- Update → an existing entity was successfully changed.
- Delete → an entity was removed or unpublished. Please note that unpublishing the entity does not remove it from the CMS, but disables it.
Once an entity is updated (new fields, new values etc), a new version is set for the entity in the CMS. New data is only available upon publishing the event! This will send an event containing the latest entity version. An “unpublish” event will contain the entity fields, as well as the version that is being unpublished.
Please keep in mind that an entity with version X can be modified → resulting in version X+1. Then, this gets unpublished. However, since there was no published version before that, you do no longer have the latest version in your database. Please also treat this corner case appropriately!
The CMS also handles confidential data, and must not be served publicly. Since the system does not provide any information about which data is of the said tier, you have to assume all data is restricted. The entities should not be publicly available. Please authenticate your endpoints so that only allowed users can access the REST API. You can use the same basic auth used for the CMS, but the users should be different. One is an organization request (the CMS sending updates), the other is user requests.
Task: Build a .NET 9 service that ingests those events, processes them, stores them in a database, and exposes them via a clean API.
Requirements:

1. Data ingestion layer
   * Expose a webhook endpoint: /cms/events
   * Secure your endpoint using Basic Authentication.
      * Username: feel free to use any string with a length of 10 to 20 characters.
      * Password: random guid.
   * Accept batch events. The first version added is version 1, and you can get multiple revisions per entity. Schema example below:

[
{ "type": "publish", "id": "X", "payload": {...}, "version": 2, "timestamp”: ”2024-01-01T00:00:00Z”},
{ "type": "delete", "id": "Y", "timestamp”: ”2024-01-01T00:00:00Z” },
{ "type": "unPublish", "id": "Z", "payload": {...}, "version": 4, "timestamp”: ”2024-01-01T00:00:00Z”},
]

2. Application Layer
   * Incoming data must be validated and sanitized.
   * Deleted entities should be removed (hard-delete), while unpublish should still keep the data in your persistence layer.
3. Data storage
   * EF Core + Relational database of your choice.
   * Entities must keep track of the latest data version.
4. REST API
   * Provide endpoints that support listing entities for consumers.
      * If the user is an admin (feel free to decide which userId/email corresponds to that of an admin), it will receive all entities that a normal user can see, including the ones that were disabled. No need to implement separate endpoints, feel free to decide how to approach this!
   * Data can not be updated by any kind of users, but an admin can disable them from the API - this will not affect the CMS, it’s an overwrite that does not affect CMS data!
5. Performance
   * Feel free to use any asynchronous mechanisms to process incoming requests. This can also be synchronous, but we would like to understand why either decision was taken.
   * Use a read-only/writer configuration for your application context and optimize your EF read queries.
6. Observability
   * Log processed events, including failing ones.
7. Testing
   * Test how events are processed and whether the ingestion constraints are successfully followed by the service.
   * Test your basic authentication mechanism with valid/invalid user-password combinations.
8. Deliverable
   * .NET Core 9 or above solution.
   * Provide a README with setup/running instructions.
   * The solution should work on either Mac or Windows, so build it platform-agnostic.
   * Github repo with all the above.

Notes to consider: This assignment is intentionally open-ended. Focus on the correctness, structure, and clarity of the system. Correct event processing is the most important part. Feel free to make use of available LLMs to help you achieve the goal proposed in this assignment!

rows.text: A publish for an unknown id creates it: published, the event's version, payload stored whole and never merged

A publish with a higher version replaces version, payload and checksum. A lower version is `ignored_stale` (`older_version`). Equal version and newer timestamp applies (state can flip back to published). Equal version and older timestamp is `ignored_stale` (`older_timestamp`)
An exact duplicate (version, instant, kind, content) is `ignored_duplicate`; replaying a whole stream changes nothing
An unPublish keeps the row and payload and marks it unpublished; users stop seeing it, admins still do
An unPublish for an id never seen (X, then X+1 unpublished with no publish between) creates the entity from the event's payload, unpublished
A delete removes the entity row and payload and leaves a payload-free tombstone (id, newest delete time). A raw-SQL check finds no `Entities` row and no content in the tombstone
Events at or before the tombstone are `ignored_stale` (`superseded_by_delete`); a newer publish recreates the entity with the admin override cleared
Delete edge cases: nothing stored gives `tombstone_only`; older than the stored state gives `newer_state_exists` but still raises the tombstone; at or below the tombstone is duplicate or stale

Order independence: every arrival order of a timeline ends in the same state. Evidence: the set-based oracle (Appendix A) on at least 20,000 seeded random timelines per run, and every permutation of at least 10 curated timelines of up to 7 events

Deterministic ties: unPublish beats publish at equal version and instant; contradicting content at equal version, instant and kind resolves to the greater payload text with `same_version_different_content`
Version is an integer ≥ 1; gaps are allowed; the first version is 1
Batch-partition independence: splitting a stream into batches any way, and applying the batches in any order, gives the same final state
An unknown event type is reported per event (`ignored_unsupported_type`), gets an `Events` row, and never fails the batch
The entity keeps the latest version; a lower or equal version never overwrites; a stale concurrent write is refused (concurrency token) and the attempt fails and retries
The admin override is its own column. CMS events never write it. A later publish does not clear it; only delete then re-create does

The ordering assumption (S17) is stated exactly in DESIGN, and the counterexample in §2.4 item 2 is pinned by a test that asserts the divergence. (Could) an applied higher version with an earlier timestamp is logged with reason `timestamp_regression`
rows.status: Done; the optional `timestamp_regression` log is not built

rows.text: `POST /cms/events` takes a JSON array; only the CMS account may call it

Basic auth. The CMS username is 10 to 20 characters and each CMS password parses as a GUID, both checked at startup (the service refuses to start otherwise). Several passwords may be active so one can be rotated without downtime

Per-event validation gives the stable reason codes in §4.5, with a boundary-pass and a boundary-fail input for every rule (id 200 and 201 characters, version 0 and 1, 7 and 8 fractional digits, the skew limit)
One bad event never blocks its neighbours. The response lists every event's outcome, reason and checksum. A batch holding only rejected events is `200`
Sanitising is normalising: trim ids, UTC timestamps, compact canonical payload, control characters rejected in ids, untrusted type text masked and bounded. Values are never altered or HTML-escaped

Limits: a declared `Content-Length` over the cap is `413` *before any body is read* (a stalled declared 10 GiB body is refused without waiting); batch of 501 is `413`; payload over 256 KiB rejects that event; depth over 32 rejects the request; invalid JSON or a non-array is `400`

Every validated publish and unPublish gets a checksum over its canonical text. It is returned in the response, stored with the entity, served by the API and recorded in the ledger. A test recomputes every stored row after a mixed workload and finds no mismatch
Status codes and `Retry-After` exactly as the §4.5 table; errors are problem+json with a stable `code` and never echo payloads
The answer follows a durable commit. A database failure at accept gives `503` and stores nothing; a `202` is never sent first
Accepting is one transaction; applying is one transaction (state, outcomes, payload purge, batch completion). A failure, crash or shutdown leaves the batch exactly as it was; nothing is half applied
A background worker applies batches, takedown batches first then oldest; it wakes on accept and polls when idle

A failing batch is retried with doubling back-off (2 s up to 60 s), set aside as `failed` after 5 attempts without blocking later batches, and can be requeued by an admin. The worker survives any exception and a storage outage
The queue is bounded by `Inbox:MaxBytes`: past it, `429 inbox_full` + `Retry-After` and nothing stored; concurrent senders cannot get past the cap
`GET /cms/batches/{id}` (CMS and admin) returns `queued`, `completed` or `failed` with per-event outcomes; never payloads; unknown id is `404`
`GET /api/admin/ingestion` reports pending batches and events, oldest age, bytes used and failed batches; requeue follows §4.2
Batches accepted before a restart are applied after it, once

A queued payload exists only in its `Events` row and is nulled in the apply transaction; the `CHECK` makes any other state impossible; a delete leaves no copy of an earlier publish in the queue or the ledger
Accepting reads no entity state; applying reads it in two queries however large the batch; the pick query uses its index with no sort

DESIGN states the choice and why: alternatives (synchronous, in-memory async, durable async), trade-offs, who calls and what each expects, the measured throughput, and what the queue does *not* do (it does not raise the single-writer ceiling)
EF Core on SQLite; one migration creates the final schema; applied at startup unless switched off
Separate write and read contexts. The read context is no-tracking, opened read-only (`Mode=ReadOnly`) and throws on `SaveChanges`. The write context is used by ingestion and the admin override only
WAL mode; writers serialised by one in-process gate; `synchronous` left at FULL; concurrency token renewed on every save
All timestamps are UTC and come back with `Kind = Utc`
The schema enforces what code assumes: the payload `CHECK`, unique (`BatchId`, `Sequence`), unique `BatchId`. A raw-SQL insert that breaks one fails
`secure_delete=ON` on every connection. After a delete (and after a payload is nulled) plus `wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)`, a unique marker string is absent from the database file and the WAL
Payload stored inline, at most `MaxPayloadBytes`; media is referenced (address, type, size, checksum), never carried
`GET /api/entities` (keyset cursor, default 50, max 100, bad cursor is `400`) and `GET /api/entities/{id}`
Users see published and not-disabled entities. Admins see everything, with a `status` block. Same endpoints; the server decides from the caller's role only; no query parameter widens it
A hidden entity returns the same `404` as a missing one
No route updates, replaces or deletes an entity. The only entity writes are admin disable and enable (idempotent, logged with who). A route-inventory test proves it
Disable changes only the override columns; payload, version and published flag are untouched and the CMS is not involved
Reads project to a DTO, track nothing, use no `Include`, write the stored payload text raw, use the partial index with no sort, and cost a constant number of queries per page
`/health` is anonymous and returns only `{"status":"ok"}` (or 503) after a database check
Responses carry `Cache-Control: no-store`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and a restrictive CSP
Deny by default: a fallback policy requires sign-in; only `/health` is anonymous. A test enumerates every mapped route and fails if one has no row in the role matrix
Least privilege exactly as the §4.6 table: the CMS cannot read entities; users and admins cannot ingest; only admins disable, enable and administer the queue
Credentials are compared in constant time (hash both sides, `FixedTimeEquals`, every account always evaluated). `401` carries `WWW-Authenticate: Basic`
Basic-auth valid and invalid combinations are covered (§6.3, suite T9)
A failed-sign-in throttle per client address answers `429` + `Retry-After`, with an injected clock
No credentials in `appsettings.json`; development credentials only in `appsettings.Development.json`; missing or malformed credentials stop startup and name the setting
No payload, password or `Authorization` header in any log, on success, rejection, 401 and failure paths; the login-failure log omits the submitted username
Production enables HTTPS redirection and HSTS; the docs say Basic auth is only safe over TLS
Hostile input is bounded: size, count, depth, strict UTF-8, control characters, far-future timestamps, lone surrogates
Admin actions are logged with who and what

Every event is logged, failing ones included, with batch id, index, id, type, version, outcome, reason and checksum. Applied and duplicate: Information. Stale, unsupported, rejected and applied-by-conflict: Warning. A failed batch: Error
The batch id is the `X-Correlation-Id` header, a property of every log line and the key in `Batches` and `Events`
`Events` is the ledger: a row per event received, rejected ones included, with `ReceivedAt` and `ProcessedAt`; no payload once decided
Meter `Lateral.Cms` with bounded tags: events processed (outcome, type), queued, apply and accept duration, queue lag, retries, set-asides, and gauges pending, oldest age and failed
Worker health is visible: a log when a batch is applied (with its wait), a Warning per failed attempt, an Error when a batch is set aside or the worker faults
DESIGN lists the alerts an operator needs, including "the CMS has gone quiet"
Event-processing tests as §6.3 suites T1, T2, T6
Ingestion-constraint tests as §6.3 suites T3, T5
Basic-auth tests as §6.3 suite T9
The suite is hermetic, finishes in under 60 s, and passes 20 consecutive full runs

rows.text: Upload: a single streamed `PUT` up to `Assets:MaxSimpleBytes`; S3-style multipart above it (initiate, parts sent in parallel, each checksummed and replaceable, complete) up to `Assets:MaxObjectBytes`. Every refusal (bad key, checksum, size, part list, expired or unknown upload) stores nothing and leaves no file
Only the CMS account uploads; the CMS and admins see an asset's state; users and admins download; only admins delete, re-scan or requeue. Every asset route has a row in the role matrix

Downloads stream with `Range` (single, suffix, open-ended; `206`, `416`), `If-Range`, `ETag` (the SHA-256) and `If-None-Match` (`304`), `HEAD`; many ranges can be read in parallel and reassemble to the original hash. Served as an attachment, typed by what the scanner detected, with `nosniff`, a sandbox CSP and `no-store`
Only a **clean** asset is ever served: quarantined, rejected and set-aside assets are the same `404` as a missing one, to users and admins alike
The store is bounded: a total cap (`429` with `Retry-After`, nothing stored, parts in flight counted), a per-object cap, and a per-caller cap on concurrent downloads

Housekeeping: unfinished uploads expire; the sweeper removes expired uploads and files no row accounts for (stray parts, quarantine files, blobs, temp files) and never takes a young file or one that is accounted for

Hard delete is physical (best effort): the row goes, the bytes are overwritten with zeros even while a reader has them open, then removed; identical content is stored once and survives until the last asset using it is deleted
Large objects are streamed, not held in memory: a 64 MiB asset is uploaded in parallel parts, scanned and downloaded while the process allocates a small fraction of its size

The mock scanner recognises, deterministically and from the bytes: a test signature (and, if switched on, EICAR); executables (disguised or bare); a declared type the bytes contradict; active content in SVG, HTML and PDF; archive bombs read from the directory alone; and simulated scanner failures. It is a stand-in that proves the pipeline, **not** protection

Pipeline: every upload is quarantined, queued, scanned by a background worker and either cleared (moved to its content address) or rejected; the scan runs outside the write gate, so a slow scan never holds up ingestion

Fail closed: a scanner error, a timeout or a missing file leaves the asset quarantined and unserved, retries with doubling back-off, and after the maximum sets it aside (still unserved) until an admin requeues it; a requeue never skips the scan
A rejected asset's bytes are overwritten and removed from disk; only its verdict, signature, checksum and times remain; assets sharing its content are rejected with it
Assets cleared by an older scanner version can be re-queued, and are not served until cleared again; an admin can re-scan any clean asset
Uploads, verdicts and admin asset actions are recorded in an append-only audit log, in the same transaction as the change, holding no content

No credential is committed: settings files hold none, and in Development without supplied credentials random ones are generated once into a git-ignored file (never in any other environment, never over supplied ones)
The memory a burst of senders can use is bounded: only `Ingestion:MaxConcurrentAccepts` batches are read at once, a queue absorbs bursts, and overflow gets `429` with `Retry-After`

The failed-sign-in throttle keys on the real client: `X-Forwarded-For` is believed only from proxies named in configuration, and ignored (so it cannot be forged to dodge the throttle) otherwise; invalid proxy settings stop startup
The test-only reset is an allow-list: it exists in Development, or in another environment only when named on purpose (`Admin:ResetAllowedEnvironment`), and never in Production
Admin actions (disable, enable, requeue, reset, asset delete and re-scan) are audited with who and what, in the same transaction; the audit log cannot be updated or deleted, and a reset keeps it
Failed batches cannot quietly fill the queue: their bytes are reported by the admin report, a gauge and the refusal log

Input that cannot be read is a `400` with a problem body in every environment, never a `500`: a bad query value, a body that is not JSON, an unknown enum value (ASP.NET throws for these in Development unless told not to). A range in a unit other than bytes is ignored
The test console, which holds live credentials, refuses to start outside Development unless told to

rows.text: The engineering console's endpoint catalogue (`endpoints.json`, which drives its API workbench and curl generator) lists exactly the routes the service maps, names the same callers the role matrix proves, and explains the responses each can give

The engineering console's Requirements page traces every original requirement in the brief to how it was met, with its tests and a live check. The brief's words are verbatim; an item is "met" only if every requirement row it cites is Done; anything partly or not met says what is missing; and the generated requirements data (`requirements.json`) matches this document

The API is described by an OpenAPI document and a Swagger page (`/swagger`) read from the routes the service really maps: each route has a name, a written summary, a group, the callers the role matrix proves can use it, and the statuses it gives; the upload routes say their body is raw bytes; the example event batch is one the service accepts. The Postman collection in `docs/postman` has a request for every route and none for a route that is gone. Both need a signed-in caller (a browser is asked for a password), the page is served under a policy that allows only its own scripts and no generated code, nothing else is relaxed, and `ApiDocs:Enabled=false` removes both

People who sign in live in the database, not in configuration. A password is stored only as a salted PBKDF2-SHA256 hash (600000 iterations by default), never in clear text, in the log or in the audit log; a hash made with fewer iterations than the setting is upgraded at the next sign-in; a malformed stored value never matches

A person signs in with a session cookie (HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, signed with keys kept on disk so a restart does not sign anyone out) as well as with Basic credentials. A wrong password, an unknown name and a disabled account get the same answer. A session ends when the password changes, the account is disabled or its sessions are revoked, including a change made straight in the database by the command-line tool

A temporary password (a first-run or administrator-made one) must be replaced before anything else is allowed: every route but sign-in, sign-out, who-am-I and change-password answers 403 `password_change_required`, for a session and for Basic credentials

An administrator creates, disables, enables, re-roles, resets (a temporary password is shown once) and deletes people. The last enabled administrator and your own account cannot be removed, disabled or demoted; a taken, malformed or weak name, role or password is refused; every change is in the audit log with the actor and no secret

A person changes their own password by proving the current one; the new one must meet the policy (12 to 128 characters, not their name, not a common one) and differ; their other sessions end and the one they are using carries on

A fresh install, with no accounts anywhere, makes one administrator with a generated temporary password written to a file beside the database (private to the service account) and not to the log; the file goes when the password is replaced; nothing is made when anybody can already sign in

The operator can manage people from the machine (`dotnet Lateral.Cms.dll admin ...`, for example over SSH): list, create, set or generate a password, change role, disable, enable, sign out, delete, make a service secret, show where data is kept. It works with the service stopped, uses the service's own rules (including the last-administrator guard) and audits as `cli:<user>`

Failed sign-ins are slowed per client address and per username (429 with `Retry-After`); a request that changes something and is authorised only by a cookie must carry a header a hostile page cannot add; a page with its own sign-in form is not given the browser's password box

The administrator can see every setting the service reads, its value now, its default, where the value came from (file, environment variable, command line or default), the environment variable that sets it and what it is for. Secrets show only as set or not set, and a password in a connection string is hidden. A setting without a description fails a test

The administrator can see where the database, asset store and session keys are, how big they are, how much room the disks have, how much of the quota is used, what to back up and where logs go; the report contains no credentials
